doc.title: Reggie Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 22, 2018

title: Junior high tuba, first improvisation, and being recruited back into band
summary: Watkins debated his future, learned basic improvisation from the band director, left band out of his high school signup, and was pulled back by the principal and band director.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: I’m going to ask a question I usually save, but when you were in let’s say junior high school were you having a debate with yourself and/or your parents about what am I going to be when I grow up?

I was having a debate with myself. Because I spent, you know band was important to me developmentally, as it is for a lot of students, musicians coming up through school. And I was in junior high and I was going through a little bit of a misbehavior phase as well because I remember myself and my friend sitting next to me would get sent to the hallway. That was the punishment in junior high, you get sent to the hallway. But at the same time they needed us, because we were the two tuba players you know. And as a junior high student I started getting made aware of jazz you know.

Basic improvisation from the band director. You know they would maybe play some things, talk about some things, and then give us some kind of basic concepts to learn how to improvise. And I remember going to my friend Matt’s house, who was a saxophone player, and doing some things, just trying — you know he had play-a-longs, and so we were checking out the play-a-longs and in band. And I didn’t really see myself as a musician actually. And at that school when you left ninth grade that was you graduated junior high in ninth grade. So while you’re getting ready to graduate you’re signing up for your high school classes. And I left band completely out. I decided I wasn’t going to be involved in it any longer you know. And it was the last couple of days of school and I guess that set off an alarm. I got called to the principal’s office.

And so I’m wondering what I did. I go to the principal’s office. He says, “So you didn’t sign up for band?” I said, “No, I’m not interested. I’m good.” He said, “Well I really think you should. They need you.” And I think I was showing a little bit of promise in terms of — become a criminal or a musician or somewhere in between. But no, so he

brought me in there specifically, just him and I, to say, “Look, you’re going to have the summer, why don’t you do band?” And I said okay. And it was a lie. You know I thought I’m not going to go. So the early August high school band camp commences and I don’t show up for band camp. Two or three days later I get a call from the band director. And he basically recruits me. And I don’t play tuba anymore and that was part of the reason, I was trying to get away from tuba. But I had shown some promise, went to All-State band and was helpful — I was a needed element to — they needed me there. They need tuba players and they need good musicians. But I just didn’t see myself as a musician.
